claim: The percentage of proliferating beta-cells in zebrafish islets at 35 dpf is 1.53% ± 0.72 (n = 5).
source: Whereas in islets from 35 dpf animals, on average 1.53% ± 0.72 (n = 5) of the beta-cells were proliferating, this number was reduced to 0.15% ± 0.07 (n = 9) and 0.06% ± 0.02 in islets from 3 mpf and 1 ypf animals, respectively (n = 10) (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by quantitative data from the FUCCI system measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The percentage of proliferating beta-cells in zebrafish islets at 3 mpf is 0.15% ± 0.07 (n = 9).
source: Whereas in islets from 35 dpf animals, on average 1.53% ± 0.72 (n = 5) of the beta-cells were proliferating, this number was reduced to 0.15% ± 0.07 (n = 9) and 0.06% ± 0.02 in islets from 3 mpf and 1 ypf animals, respectively (n = 10) (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by quantitative data from the FUCCI system measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The percentage of proliferating beta-cells in zebrafish islets at 1 ypf is 0.06% ± 0.02 (n = 10).
source: Whereas in islets from 35 dpf animals, on average 1.53% ± 0.72 (n = 5) of the beta-cells were proliferating, this number was reduced to 0.15% ± 0.07 (n = 9) and 0.06% ± 0.02 in islets from 3 mpf and 1 ypf animals, respectively (n = 10) (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by quantitative data from the FUCCI system measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Beta-cell proliferation declines with advancing age in zebrafish.
source: We found that the percentage of proliferating beta-cells declined with advancing age.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing decreasing proliferation rates across different age groups.

claim: A similar decline in beta-cell proliferation was observed in secondary islets.
source: A similar decline in beta-cell proliferation was observed also in the secondary islets, which arise from the differentiation of sox9b-expressing progenitors lining the pancreatic ducts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from secondary islets shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Adult beta-cells in zebrafish primary islets are functional and sensitive to glucose.
source: We found that adult beta-cells were sensitive to glucose, as beta-cells exhibited calcium influx upon stimulation with increasing glucose concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging experiments using GCaMP6s.

claim: 74 genes showed 1.5-log2fold difference (p<0.05) in expression between beta-cells from 3 mpf and 1 ypf zebrafish.
source: A comparison between beta-cells from 3 mpf and 1 ypf animals revealed 74 genes that showed 1.5-log2fold difference (p<0.05) in expression (Figure 2b), of which 61 genes were upregulated and 13 genes were downregulated in older beta-cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by RNA-sequencing data comparing two age groups.

claim: 61 genes were upregulated in beta-cells from 1 ypf compared to 3 mpf zebrafish.
source: A comparison between beta-cells from 3 mpf and 1 ypf animals revealed 74 genes that showed 1.5-log2fold difference (p<0.05) in expression (Figure 2b), of which 61 genes were upregulated and 13 genes were downregulated in older beta-cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by RNA-sequencing data.

claim: 13 genes were downregulated in beta-cells from 1 ypf compared to 3 mpf zebrafish.
source: A comparison between beta-cells from 3 mpf and 1 ypf animals revealed 74 genes that showed 1.5-log2fold difference (p<0.05) in expression (Figure 2b), of which 61 genes were upregulated and 13 genes were downregulated in older beta-cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by RNA-sequencing data.

claim: Upregulated genes in older beta-cells are involved in the negative regulation of growth-factor signaling including socs2, cish, spry4 and fstl1.
source: Literature survey and unbiased gene ontology analysis using DAVID (Huang et al., 2009a; Huang et al., 2009b) revealed that the upregulated genes were involved in the negative regulation of growth-factor signaling including socs2, cish, spry4 and fstl1 (Figure 2c–c').
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data using DAVID.

claim: Upregulated genes in older beta-cells include genes involved in ER stress including trib3 and cebpd.
source: We also found upregulation of genes involved in ER stress including trib3 and cebpd, as well as genes associated with increased risk of developing Type two diabetes and glucose intolerance (prtfa, lpp and socs2) (Fang et al., 2014; Szabat et al., 2016; Kato et al., 2006; Lebrun et al., 2010; Nair et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and literature citations.

claim: Upregulated genes in older beta-cells include genes associated with increased risk of developing Type two diabetes and glucose intolerance (prtfa, lpp and socs2).
source: We also found upregulation of genes involved in ER stress including trib3 and cebpd, as well as genes associated with increased risk of developing Type two diabetes and glucose intolerance (prtfa, lpp and socs2) (Fang et al., 2014; Szabat et al., 2016; Kato et al., 2006; Lebrun et al., 2010; Nair et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and literature citations linking these genes to diabetes risk.

claim: Cytokine-mediated signaling was over-represented in gene ontology analysis of genes upregulated in older beta-cells.
source: In addition to the genes involved in regulating proliferation and ER stress, cytokine-mediated signaling was over-represented in the gene ontology analysis performed using DAVID (Figure 2c').
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Transcripts associated with an inflammatory signature, such as interleukins, complement factors and members of the NF-kB pathway, including il15, c9, tnfrsf1b, cd74a, cd74b increased in expression in islets from older animals.
source: We found that transcripts associated with an inflammatory signature, such as interleukins, complement factors and members of the NF-kB pathway, including il15, c9, tnfrsf1b, cd74a, cd74b (Starlets et al., 2006), also increased in expression in islets from older animals (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and literature citation.

claim: tnfrsf1b belongs to a superfamily of cytokine receptors, which respond to Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) and activate NF-kB.
source: Specifically, tnfrsf1b belongs to a superfamily of cytokine receptors, which respond to Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) and activate NF-kB, an inducible and ubiquitous transcription factor that senses inflammation (Espı´nEspín-Palazo´nPalazón et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation describing the function of tnfrsf1b.

claim: NF-kB is an inducible and ubiquitous transcription factor that senses inflammation.
source: Specifically, tnfrsf1b belongs to a superfamily of cytokine receptors, which respond to Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) and activate NF-kB, an inducible and ubiquitous transcription factor that senses inflammation (Espı´nEspín-Palazo´nPalazón et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation and established scientific knowledge.

claim: There was an increase in the proportion of beta-cells expressing tnfrsf1b in islets of older animals.
source: Notably, the single-cell RT-qPCR revealed that there was an increase in the proportion of beta-cells expressing tnfrsf1b in islets of older animals (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RT-qPCR data.

claim: The proportion of beta-cells expressing ikbaa and tnfα increased in islets of older animals.
source: This was also true for additional components of the NF-kB pathway, including ikbaa and tnfα.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RT-qPCR data.

claim: The proportion of sorted cells expressing known beta-cell markers such as insulin, islet1 and neurod1, remained similar between 3 mpf and 1 ypf.
source: In contrast, the proportion of sorted cells expressing known beta-cell markers such as insulin, islet1 and neurod1, remained similar (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RT-qPCR data.

claim: 32.2% ± 32.07 beta-cells (n = 6) in tnfrsf1b-injected animals expressed GFP at 5 dpf.
source: A total of 32.2% ± 32.07 beta-cells (n = 6) in the tnfrsf1b-injected animals expressed GFP as compared to 2.4% ± 1.98 beta-cells (n = 5) in the controls (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mosaic overexpression experiments.

claim: 2.4% ± 1.98 beta-cells (n = 5) in control animals expressed GFP at 5 dpf.
source: A total of 32.2% ± 32.07 beta-cells (n = 6) in the tnfrsf1b-injected animals expressed GFP as compared to 2.4% ± 1.98 beta-cells (n = 5) in the controls (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from control experiments.

claim: Overexpressing tnfrsf1b in beta-cells can induce NF-kB signaling.
source: We saw that a higher proportion of beta-cells from animals injected with ins:tnfrsf1b expressed GFP at 5 dpf compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased NF-kB reporter activity upon tnfrsf1b overexpression.

claim: GFP intensity was too low to be detected in beta-cells from the primary or secondary islets of juveniles (1 mpf).
source: We found that GFP intensity was too low to be detected in beta-cells from the primary or secondary islets of juveniles (1 mpf) (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data of NF-kB reporter expression.

claim: Beta-cells from 3 mpf animals exhibited a detectable, salt-and-pepper pattern of GFP expression.
source: In contrast, beta-cells from 3 mpf animals exhibited a detectable, salt-and-pepper pattern of GFP expression (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), suggesting heterogeneous NF-kB activation, which is consistent with the heterogeneous expression of tnfrsf1b (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data and is consistent with gene expression data.

claim: Nearly all beta-cells in both the primary and secondary islets from 1 ypf animals express GFP.
source: Notably, nearly all beta-cells in both the primary and secondary islets from 1 ypf animals express GFP (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data of NF-kB reporter expression.

claim: A higher proportion of cells express GFP in older animals compared to younger animals.
source: Quantifying the proportion of cells within the low- and high-GFP expressing regions indicated that a higher proportion of cells express GFP in older animals (Figure 3f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis.

claim: The overall GFP expression increases in individual cells with increasing age.
source: Thus, we found that not only does the overall GFP expression increases in individual cells with increasing age, but a higher proportion of cells with GFP expression were present in the islets of the older compared to younger animals (Figure 3f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis.

claim: There was approximately 50% increase in the GFP transcript levels in beta-cells from 1 ypf animals as compared to 3 mpf animals.
source: We saw approximately 50% increase in the GFP transcript levels in beta-cells from 1 ypf animals as compared to 3 mpf animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: There was a positive correlation between GFP mRNA and GFP fluorescence intensity across cells (R2 = 0.28).
source: Overall, there was a positive correlation between GFP mRNA and GFP fluorescence intensity across cells (R2 = 0.28) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by index sorting and single-cell RT-qPCR data.

claim: Innate immune cells were not present in the islets during the larval stages (15–21 dpf).
source: We found that whereas innate immune cells were not present in the islets during the larval stages (15–21 dpf), they had infiltrated them during the late juvenile stages (45 dpf) (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data using L-plastin marker.

claim: Innate immune cells had infiltrated the islets during the late juvenile stages (45 dpf).
source: We found that whereas innate immune cells were not present in the islets during the larval stages (15–21 dpf), they had infiltrated them during the late juvenile stages (45 dpf) (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data using L-plastin marker.

claim: The innate immune cells in the islets were macrophages.
source: Analysis of the macrophage reporter line, Tg(mpeg1:mCherry), revealed that the innate immune cells were macrophages, whereas neutrophils could not be detected, as assessed by the neutrophil-specific line Tg(lyz2:GFP) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of macrophage reporter line.

claim: Neutrophils could not be detected in the islets.
source: Analysis of the macrophage reporter line, Tg(mpeg1:mCherry), revealed that the innate immune cells were macrophages, whereas neutrophils could not be detected, as assessed by the neutrophil-specific line Tg(lyz2:GFP) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of neutrophil-specific reporter line.

claim: On average 25% ± 10.9 (n = 5) of the L-plastin-positive cells inside the islet expressed tnfα:GFP in 3 mpf animals.
source: On average 25% ± 10.9 (n = 5) and 17% ± 11.1 (n = 5) of the L-plastin-positive cells inside the islet expressed tnfα:GFP in 3 mpf and one ypf animals, respectively (p>0.05) (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of tnfα:GFP expression in immune cells.

claim: On average 17% ± 11.1 (n = 5) of the L-plastin-positive cells inside the islet expressed tnfα:GFP in 1 ypf animals.
source: On average 25% ± 10.9 (n = 5) and 17% ± 11.1 (n = 5) of the L-plastin-positive cells inside the islet expressed tnfα:GFP in 3 mpf and one ypf animals, respectively (p>0.05) (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of tnfα:GFP expression in immune cells.

claim: The tnfα:GFP-expressing leukocytes were macrophages.
source: Analysis of TgBAC(tnfα:GFP) together with specific labeling of macrophages using Tg(mpeg1:mCherry) confirmed that the tnfα:GFP-expressing leukocytes were macrophages (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-labeling experiments with macrophage-specific markers.

claim: tnfα-expression alone could induce NF-kB:GFP reporter activity.
source: Indeed, we found that tnfα-expression alone could induce NF-kB:GFP reporter activity (Figure 4d–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by mosaic overexpression experiments.

claim: A lower proportion of the NF-kB:GFPhigh cells had incorporated EdU over a 2-day period as compared to GFPlow cells.
source: We observed that a lower proportion of the NF-kB:GFPhigh cells had incorporated EdU over a 2-day period as compared to GFPlow cells (Figure 5a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data.

claim: The GFP fluorescence of beta-cells remains stable over a 2-day period.
source: In order to confirm that the GFP fluorescence of beta-cells remains stable over the 2-day period of EdU incorporation, we followed individual FAC-sorted NF-kB:GFPhigh and low beta-cells over 72 hr ex vivo. Indeed, the GFP fluorescence remained stable over the time-period of the experiment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging of sorted cells.

claim: A higher proportion of NF-kB:GFPlow cells were positive for PCNA, as compared to NF-kB:GFPhigh cells.
source: A higher proportion of NF-kB:GFPlow cells were positive for PCNA, as compared to NF-kB:GFPhigh cells (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCNA immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Beta-cells with high NF-kB signaling proliferate significantly less compared to their neighbors with lower activity.
source: We conclude that beta-cells with high NF-kB signaling proliferate significantly less compared to their neighbors with lower activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU and PCNA data showing reduced proliferation in GFPhigh cells.

claim: socs2 showed more than 2.5-fold higher expression in the GFPhigh cells compared to GFPlow.
source: We found that socs2 showed more than 2.5-fold higher expression (n = 4 biological replicates, n = 3 animals per replicate, 1000 cells per condition) in the GFPhigh cells compared to GFPlow, whereas other genes did not exhibit significantly higher expression (Figure 6b, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RT-qPCR data comparing GFPhigh and GFPlow populations.

claim: 8.44% ± 3.37 of the CFP-negative beta-cells were proliferating at 23–25 dpf.
source: We found that whereas 8.44% ± 3.37 of the CFP-negative beta-cells were proliferating, only 1.08% ± 1.65 CFP-positive beta-cells exhibited cell-cycle progression (n = 9) (Figure 6e).
evidence: The claim is supported by FUCCI analysis of mosaic overexpression experiments.

claim: Only 1.08% ± 1.65 CFP-positive beta-cells exhibited cell-cycle progression at 23–25 dpf.
source: We found that whereas 8.44% ± 3.37 of the CFP-negative beta-cells were proliferating, only 1.08% ± 1.65 CFP-positive beta-cells exhibited cell-cycle progression (n = 9) (Figure 6e).
evidence: The claim is supported by FUCCI analysis of mosaic overexpression experiments.

claim: Overexpression of CFP alone, or CFP-T2A-rapgef4 and CFP-T2A-spry4 in a mosaic manner did not affect proliferation.
source: Overexpression of CFP alone, or CFP-T2A-rapgef4 and CFP-T2A-spry4 in this mosaic manner did not affect proliferation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments showing no effect on proliferation.

claim: socs2 can cell-autonomously inhibit beta-cell proliferation.
source: Thus, socs2 can cell-autonomously inhibit beta-cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by mosaic overexpression experiments showing reduced proliferation in socs2-expressing cells.

claim: The aging islets exhibit signs of chronic inflammation including recruitment of tnfα-expressing macrophages.
source: By comparing beta-cells from younger and older zebrafish, here we show that the aging islets exhibit signs of chronic inflammation. These include recruitment of tnfα-expressing macrophages and the activation of NF-kB signaling in beta-cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and gene expression data showing macrophage infiltration and tnfα expression.

claim: The aging islets exhibit signs of chronic inflammation including the activation of NF-kB signaling in beta-cells.
source: By comparing beta-cells from younger and older zebrafish, here we show that the aging islets exhibit signs of chronic inflammation. These include recruitment of tnfα-expressing macrophages and the activation of NF-kB signaling in beta-cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by NF-kB reporter data and gene expression analysis.

claim: NF-kB activity is undetectable in juvenile beta-cells.
source: Using a transgenic reporter, we show that NF-kB activity is undetectable in juvenile beta-cells, whereas cells from older fish exhibit heterogeneous NF-kB activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging of NF-kB reporter expression.

claim: Cells from older fish exhibit heterogeneous NF-kB activity.
source: Using a transgenic reporter, we show that NF-kB activity is undetectable in juvenile beta-cells, whereas cells from older fish exhibit heterogeneous NF-kB activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging of NF-kB reporter expression showing salt-and-pepper pattern.

claim: The NF-kB signalinghi cells exhibit premature upregulation of socs2.
source: The NF-kB signalinghi cells also exhibit premature upregulation of socs2, an age-related gene that inhibits beta-cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data comparing GFPhigh and GFPlow populations.

claim: socs2 is an age-related gene that inhibits beta-cell proliferation.
source: The NF-kB signalinghi cells also exhibit premature upregulation of socs2, an age-related gene that inhibits beta-cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing age-related upregulation and functional experiments showing proliferation inhibition.

claim: NF-kB activity marks the asynchronous decline in beta-cell proliferation with advancing age.
source: Together, our results show that NF-kB activity marks the asynchronous decline in beta-cell proliferation with advancing age.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing heterogeneous NF-kB activity correlating with proliferative differences.

claim: Aging is a universal process that detrimentally changes the characteristics of cells in multicellular organisms.
source: Aging is a universal process that detrimentally changes the characteristics of cells in multicellular organisms.
evidence: The claim represents established scientific knowledge about aging.

claim: A hallmark of aging is the reduction in cellular renewal and proliferation across different tissues and organs.
source: A hallmark of aging is the reduction in cellular renewal and proliferation across different tissues and organs (Yun, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Young beta-cells are highly proliferative and increase rapidly in number from the prenatal phase until early stages of development in mammals.
source: Whereas young beta-cell are highly proliferative and increase rapidly in number from the prenatal phase until early stages of development in mammals, beta-cell proliferation becomes dramatically reduced in adults (Perl et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Beta-cell proliferation becomes dramatically reduced in adults.
source: Whereas young beta-cell are highly proliferative and increase rapidly in number from the prenatal phase until early stages of development in mammals, beta-cell proliferation becomes dramatically reduced in adults (Perl et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Adult beta-cell proliferation can increase under specific conditions such as obesity and pregnancy.
source: Nevertheless, adult beta-cell proliferation can increase under specific conditions such as obesity and pregnancy (Parsons et al., 1992; Weir et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Rejuvenating the beta-cell environment by implanting old islets in younger animals is sufficient to restore the proliferative potential of the aged beta-cells.
source: For example, rejuvenating the beta-cell environment by implanting old islets in younger animals is sufficient to restore the proliferative potential of the aged beta-cells (Almaça et al., 2014; Salpeter et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Transcriptome and methylome studies revealed age-dependent DNA methylation changes at cell-cycle regulators, which may contribute to the quiescence of aging beta-cells.
source: In addition, transcriptome and methylome studies revealed age-dependent DNA methylation changes at cell-cycle regulators, which may contribute to the quiescence of aging beta-cells (Avrahami et al., 2015; Arda et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations and involves speculation about mechanism.

claim: Analysis of gene expression in islets from aging mice showed an age-dependent decline of transcripts encoding the platelet-derived growth factor-receptors Pdgfra and Pdgfrb as well as its ligand Pdgf.
source: Furthermore, analysis of gene expression in islets from aging mice showed an age-dependent decline of transcripts encoding the platelet-derived growth factor-receptors Pdgfra and Pdgfrb as well as its ligand Pdgf. This decline in expression was shown to underlie a decline in beta-cell proliferation with aging (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The decline in expression of Pdgfra, Pdgfrb and Pdgf was shown to underlie a decline in beta-cell proliferation with aging.
source: Furthermore, analysis of gene expression in islets from aging mice showed an age-dependent decline of transcripts encoding the platelet-derived growth factor-receptors Pdgfra and Pdgfrb as well as its ligand Pdgf. This decline in expression was shown to underlie a decline in beta-cell proliferation with aging (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The expression of the transcription factor FoxM1 declines with aging.
source: Likewise, the expression of the transcription factor FoxM1 declines with aging and the forced expression of its activated form in aged beta-cells is sufficient to re-ignite replication (Golson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The forced expression of activated FoxM1 in aged beta-cells is sufficient to re-ignite replication.
source: Likewise, the expression of the transcription factor FoxM1 declines with aging and the forced expression of its activated form in aged beta-cells is sufficient to re-ignite replication (Golson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The prostaglandin receptors (E-Prostanoid Receptor 3 and 4) might regulate beta-cell proliferation in an age-dependent manner.
source: In addition, the prostaglandin receptors (E-Prostanoid Receptor 3 and 4) might also regulate beta-cell proliferation in an age-dependent manner (Carboneau et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation and involves speculation.

claim: Beta-cells within the islet and between islets may belong to subpopulations with different 'ages'.
source: In particular, beta-cells within the islet and between islets may belong to subpopulations with different 'ages' (van der Meulen et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2017), with the proportion of young-to-old beta-cells changing with the age of the animal (Aguayo-Mazzucato et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: The proportion of young-to-old beta-cells changes with the age of the animal.
source: In particular, beta-cells within the islet and between islets may belong to subpopulations with different 'ages' (van der Meulen et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2017), with the proportion of young-to-old beta-cells changing with the age of the animal (Aguayo-Mazzucato et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Recent studies have identified various markers of beta-cell heterogeneity such as Fltp, ST8SIA1 and CD9.
source: In addition, recent studies have identified various markers of beta-cell heterogeneity such as Fltp, ST8SIA1 and CD9 (Bader et al., 2016; Dorrell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Fltp was shown to distinguish the proliferative beta-cells from the more functional ones.
source: Specifically, Fltp was shown to distinguish the proliferative beta-cells from the more functional ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from cited literature.

claim: There is emerging evidence that chronic inflammation is a characteristic of aging in human.
source: There is emerging evidence that chronic inflammation is a characteristic of aging in human (Puchta et al., 2016) and is associated with beta-cell dysfunction in type two diabetes (Nordmann et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Chronic inflammation is associated with beta-cell dysfunction in type two diabetes.
source: There is emerging evidence that chronic inflammation is a characteristic of aging in human (Puchta et al., 2016) and is associated with beta-cell dysfunction in type two diabetes (Nordmann et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Islets from older human donors exhibit an increase in the number of intra-islet macrophages.
source: Furthermore, islets form older human donors exhibit an increase in the number of intra-islet macrophages (Almaça et al., 2014), analogous to zebrafish.
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: A recent report revealed progressive increases in the proportion of beta cells expressing age-related markers, including IGF-IR in older mice and human islets.
source: A recent report from Bonner-Weir and colleagues (Aguayo-Mazzucato et al., 2017) revealed progressive increases in the proportion of beta cells expressing age-related markers, including IGF-IR in older mice and human islets, suggesting that aging in mammalian beta-cells might be a heterogeneous process.
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Aging in mammalian beta-cells might be a heterogeneous process.
source: A recent report from Bonner-Weir and colleagues (Aguayo-Mazzucato et al., 2017) revealed progressive increases in the proportion of beta cells expressing age-related markers, including IGF-IR in older mice and human islets, suggesting that aging in mammalian beta-cells might be a heterogeneous process.
evidence: The claim involves speculation based on cited evidence.

claim: The human receptor TNFRSF11A (Receptor Activator of NF-kB) shows markedly heterogeneous expression in adult human beta-cells according to single-cell sequencing database.
source: Intriguingly, the human receptor TNFRSF11A (Receptor Activator of NF-kB) shows markedly heterogeneous expression in adult human beta-cells according to the single-cell sequencing database provided by the Sandberg lab (http://sandberg.cmb.ki.se/pancreas/) (Segerstolpe et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation and database reference.

claim: TNFRSF11A antagonism can increase human beta-cell proliferation.
source: Notably, TNFRSF11A antagonism can increase human beta-cell proliferation, implicating NF-kB signaling in beta-cell proliferation (Kondegowda et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Adenovirus transduction of socs3 in rat islets inhibits beta-cell proliferation.
source: Of note, adenovirus transduction of the functionally related gene socs3 in rat islets inhibits beta-cell proliferation (Lindberg et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Gene-expression analysis revealed that proliferating beta-cells reduce the levels of transcripts required for beta-cell function.
source: For example, gene-expression analysis revealed that proliferating beta-cells reduce the levels of transcripts required for beta-cell function (Klochendler et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Lineage tracing of immature and mature beta-cells within the same islet revealed higher proliferation of immature beta-cells.
source: In addition, lineage tracing of immature and mature beta-cells within the same islet revealed higher proliferation of immature beta-cells (Singh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: A recent report documented the presence of islet-resident macrophages expressing TNFα, IL1b and MHC-II in non-obese diabetic (NOD) mice.
source: In agreement with our findings, a recent report documented the presence of islet-resident macrophages expressing TNFα, IL1b and MHC-II (Ferris et al., 2017) in non-obese diabetic (NOD) mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Ferris et al. could not detect nuclear RelA signaling in the islets of NOD mice.
source: However, despite the presence of cytokine expression in the macrophages, Ferris et al. could not detect nuclear RelA (a member of the NF-kB heterodimer) signaling in the islets, suggesting that beta-cells did not activate NF-kB signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Acinar cells were recently shown to express TNFα, which in turn induces apoptosis in aged mouse beta-cells.
source: For example, acinar cells were recently shown to express TNFα, which in turn induces apoptosis in aged mouse beta-cells (Xiong et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: ER stress is known to activate NF-kB signaling in multiple cell types.
source: In particular, ER stress is known to activate NF-kB signaling in multiple cell types (Tam et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: With aging, beta-cells may experience higher levels of ER stress and thereby activate NF-kB signaling.
source: It is possible that with aging, beta-cells experience higher levels of ER stress and thereby activate NF-kB signaling.
evidence: The claim involves speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: The higher endogenous expression of socs2 in NF-kB:GFPhigh compared to NF-kB:GFPlow beta-cells could contribute to the proliferative heterogeneity among beta-cells based on the differences in NF-kB signaling strength.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the higher endogenous expression of socs2 in NF-kB:GFPhigh compared to NF-kB:GFPlow beta-cells could contribute to the proliferative heterogeneity among beta-cells based on the differences in NF-kB signaling strength.
evidence: The claim involves inference and speculation based on experimental data.

evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation and established knowledge about beta-cell zinc content.
